# 01 Recommendation Systems & Motivation {background-color="#EF7C00"}

## Why recommend anything?

- Digital services offer more items than any person can inspect.
- A recommender narrows a large choice set into a ranked, actionable set of options.
- The ranking is never neutral: it determines what receives attention and what remains unseen.

::: notes
Open by asking students to name one recommendation they acted on this week. Use the examples to define the problem as helping a user choose from a large catalogue.
:::

## Recommendation systems are everywhere

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Inputs**

- user behaviour and context
- item attributes
- social or collaborative signals
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Outputs**

- a shortlist
- a ranking
- an exposure decision
:::
:::

The system translates signals into a choice architecture for the user.

::: notes
Use familiar examples such as videos, music, shopping, news, jobs, and course resources. Keep the emphasis on the general pattern rather than any one platform.
:::

## Objectives shape exposure

- Optimising **click-through** may favour surprising or sensational items.
- Optimising **completion** may favour familiar items.
- Optimising **diversity** may increase discovery but reduce short-term relevance.

::: {.callout-warning}
The technical objective is also a social choice: it affects users, creators, and communities differently.
:::

::: notes
Ask: “If two systems use the same data but optimise different objectives, should we expect the same recommendations?” Take two responses before stating no.
:::

## Ethics Thread: who gets seen?

- Recommendations shape what people read, watch, buy, apply for, and notice.
- Exposure can accumulate through feedback loops.
- We will revisit **bias, fairness, privacy, transparency, and stakeholder impact** every week.

::: notes
Connect this thread to the course promise: technical design and ethical analysis are taught together, not as separate topics.
:::

## A card-suit framework for user types

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
♠ **Explorer** — novelty, diversity, serendipity

♥ **Social connector** — community and shared taste
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
♦ **Pragmatist** — precise, task-oriented results

♣ **Loyalist** — familiar items and consistency
:::
:::

Users can move between archetypes depending on the task and context.

::: notes
Invite students to choose an archetype for one service they use. Do not present the archetypes as a scientific taxonomy; they are a prompt for thinking about objectives.
:::

## Matching systems to user needs

| User need | Plausible approach | Objective |
|---|---|---|
| Explorer | Diversity-aware or serendipity models | Novelty, coverage |
| Social connector | Collaborative filtering or social graphs | Community similarity |
| Pragmatist | Retrieval and ranking | Precision, relevance |
| Loyalist | Content-based filtering | Consistency, familiarity |

::: notes
Close the first segment by stressing that the same platform may need several approaches at once.
:::

# 03 Classical Recommendation Methods {background-color="#EF7C00"}

## Formulating a recommendation problem

1. **Who** is the user or stakeholder?
2. **What** item, action, or outcome is being recommended?
3. **Which signals** are available at decision time?
4. **What objective** determines the ranking?

::: notes
Work through one example, such as recommending course readings, and distinguish the objective from the implementation method.
:::

## Popularity-based recommendation

- Recommend globally popular items.
- Requires little or no user history.
- Useful as a baseline and a cold-start fallback.
- Risks reinforcing existing exposure inequalities.

::: notes
Ask students why a baseline can be useful even when it is not personalised.
:::

## Content-based filtering

- Represent items using features or metadata.
- Recommend items similar to what a user previously liked.
- Works when item features are rich and interpretable.
- Can over-specialise and repeat the user’s existing taste.

::: notes
Use a concrete example: recommending films from genre, director, language, and cast features.
:::

## Collaborative filtering

- Learn from patterns shared across users or items.
- Does not require detailed item features.
- Can surface unexpected items through similar users.
- Depends on sufficient interaction data and inherits its biases.

::: notes
Contrast “similar item features” with “similar behaviour” before introducing matrix factorisation next week.
:::

## Hybrid approaches

Combine signals when no single paradigm is reliable:

- content features for new items;
- collaborative signals for personalisation;
- popularity for robust fallbacks;
- business or safety constraints for deployment.

::: notes
Emphasise that production systems are usually pipelines or hybrids rather than one textbook method.
:::

## The cold-start problem

| Cold-start case | What is missing? | Typical response |
|---|---|---|
| New user | Interaction history | Onboarding questions or popularity fallback |
| New item | Ratings or clicks | Content features or exploration |
| New system | Both users and items | Carefully designed defaults and data collection |

::: notes
Use the table to distinguish the three cases. Ask which strategy creates the most risk of a popularity feedback loop.
:::

## Exposure and feedback loops

- Recommendations create exposure.
- Exposure creates interactions.
- Interactions become training data.
- Training data then changes future exposure.

::: {.callout-warning}
Offline success can hide who is systematically left out of the loop.
:::

::: notes
Connect the loop to popularity bias, new entrants, niche creators, and minority preferences.
:::

## Ethics Thread: Popularity Bias and Exposure Inequality

- Popular items receive more recommendations and more interaction.
- Long-tail items may never accumulate enough signal to compete.
- Engagement-only objectives can disadvantage creators and communities with less historical exposure.

::: notes
Invite two students to identify stakeholders who would evaluate this system differently.
:::

## Summary

🤞 <u>Recommendation design is objective design.</u>

| Method | Personalised? | Item features? | New-item friendly? |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Popularity | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ |
| Content-based | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Collaborative filtering | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ |
| Hybrid | ✓ | Often | Partial |

:::
